title: Transforms and physics from jobs
sub: TransformAccessArray, IJobParallelForTransform and batched physics queries instead of thousands of calls
cards/0/title: Unity objects are not allowed in jobs
cards/0/body:
GameObject, Transform, GetComponent, Physics.Raycast, Time.time are main-thread API, and engine objects are managed. You cannot touch them in a job, let alone in Burst code.

Yet the most common bulk operations in a game are moving transforms and casting rays. For these Unity offers two official ways out:

  • TransformAccessArray + IJobParallelForTransform — reading and writing transforms on worker threads;
  • batched physics queries — RaycastCommand and its relatives: thousands of queries in one call, executed in jobs.

This is the built-in physics (PhysX, the UnityEngine.PhysicsModule module), not the Unity Physics package for Entities.
cards/1/body:
TransformAccessArray is a native list of transforms. Create it once from an array (new TransformAccessArray(transforms)) or grow it with Add and RemoveAtSwapBack. It is native memory, so Dispose() is mandatory.

An IJobParallelForTransform job gets Execute(int index, TransformAccess transform). TransformAccess has position, rotation, localPosition, localRotation, localScale, the matrices, SetPositionAndRotation and isValid. The index matches the index in the array — use it to read your own data from a NativeArray.

Anything you need from main-thread API (time, input) you compute up front and pass in a field. Schedule with Schedule(transforms) in Update, complete in LateUpdate, and in OnDestroy call Complete() first, then Dispose().
cards/2/title: The trap: only different roots run in parallel
cards/2/body:
The writing Schedule(transforms) parallelizes work across different hierarchies. Transforms that share a root object are always processed on the same thread: Unity does not let two threads write into one hierarchy.

So 10 000 enemies parented under one Enemies object “to keep the hierarchy tidy” will run on a single thread. You get Burst, but no parallelism. The fix is to keep objects that move in bulk at the scene root, or to split them across several roots.

If you only need to read — gather positions for another job — there is ScheduleReadOnly(transforms, batchSize): it reads all transforms in parallel regardless of the hierarchy. A transform may have been destroyed there, so check isValid. For debugging there is RunReadOnly; this job has no plain Run.
cards/3/q: 10 000 enemies are children of one Enemies object. An IJobParallelForTransform with [BurstCompile] moves them via Schedule(transforms), and the Profiler Timeline shows the job on a single worker thread. Why?
cards/3/options/0: All the transforms share a root, and the writing Schedule only parallelizes different hierarchies
cards/3/options/2: IJobParallelForTransform always runs on one thread
cards/3/explain: Transforms with a shared root are processed by one thread. Move the enemies to the scene root or split them across several roots, and the work spreads over the workers. If you only read, ScheduleReadOnly parallelizes regardless of the hierarchy.
cards/3/wrong/1: Without ScheduleBatchedJobs the job starts later, but it is still handed out to the workers.
cards/3/wrong/2: With different roots the work is split across the worker threads.
cards/3/wrong/3: Vectorization is about instructions within a thread; it has nothing to do with the thread count.
cards/4/q: What can you do inside Execute(int i, TransformAccess t) of an IJobParallelForTransform? Select all that apply.
cards/4/options/4: Read a speed from a [ReadOnly] NativeArray at index i
cards/4/explain: TransformAccess gives position, rotation, scale and SetPositionAndRotation, and the job reads its own data from native containers by index. Time and GetComponent are main-thread API: time is passed in a field, and components are not reachable from a job.
cards/5/title: RaycastCommand: hundreds of rays in one call
cards/5/body:
Instead of a loop of Physics.Raycast, build a batch:

  • a NativeArray<RaycastCommand> — one command per ray: new RaycastCommand(from, direction, queryParameters, distance);
  • a NativeArray<RaycastHit> of size commands × maxHits;
  • RaycastCommand.ScheduleBatch(commands, results, minCommandsPerJob, maxHits, dependsOn) — it returns a JobHandle.

The rays run in jobs, in parallel with each other. minCommandsPerJob is the minimum number of commands per job, much like batchSize. Until Complete() is called, results is off-limits.

QueryParameters (since 2022.2) sets the layer mask, triggers, back faces and multiple hits per mesh; there is QueryParameters.Default. The old constructors taking layerMask and maxHits are deprecated: maxHits now goes to ScheduleBatch, and without it it is 1.
cards/6/title: Reading the results and building a chain
cards/6/body:
The results of command N start at index N × maxHits. If there are fewer hits than maxHits, the first empty result is marked by collider == null — stop there. The command does not overwrite the slots after it, so they may hold garbage from last time.

hit.collider is a managed object, so you read it on the main thread. The numbers — point, normal, distance — can be processed in a following job too.

You can fill the commands in a Burst job and pass its JobHandle as dependsOn — that gives a chain with no Complete() in the middle. If you cast rays every frame, do not reallocate the buffers: create them once with Allocator.Persistent in Awake and free them in OnDestroy. In the Profiler the batch shows up as BatchQuery.ExecuteRaycastJob.

SpherecastCommand, BoxcastCommand, CapsulecastCommand, ClosestPointCommand (since 2022.1) and OverlapSphereCommand, OverlapBoxCommand, OverlapCapsuleCommand (since 2022.2, results are ColliderHit) work the same way.
cards/7/q: Put one frame with a batch of rays in order.
cards/7/items/0: Allocate a NativeArray<RaycastCommand> and a NativeArray<RaycastHit> of commands × maxHits
cards/7/items/1: Fill the commands: new RaycastCommand(from, direction, query, distance)
cards/7/items/3: The main thread does its own work while the rays run in jobs
cards/7/items/4: Complete() and read the results up to the first collider == null
cards/7/explain: Buffers and commands first, then one call to schedule the batch. While the rays fly, the main thread is free. Read the results only after Complete(), and free the memory only after that.
cards/8/task: Replace the 500 Physics.Raycast calls in GroundProbe with one batch. In Update, fill commands with new RaycastCommand(..., QueryParameters, 10f) and schedule RaycastCommand.ScheduleBatch(commands, results, 32, 1), keeping the JobHandle in a field. In LateUpdate, call Complete() and update groundY only where collider != null. In OnDestroy, wait for the batch before Dispose().
cards/8/checks/0/label: The JobHandle is a field, and Update assigns it RaycastCommand.ScheduleBatch(commands, results, ...)
cards/8/checks/1/label: Update fills the commands with new RaycastCommand using QueryParameters
cards/8/checks/4/label: LateUpdate calls Complete() first, then checks collider != null
cards/8/checks/5/label: In OnDestroy, Complete() comes before Dispose()
cards/8/explain: The 500 rays go out as one batch and run on worker threads while the rest of the frame executes. The buffers are Persistent, allocated once. Without Complete() in OnDestroy, the batch could write into results after Dispose(). To take the filling off the main thread too, build the commands in a Burst job and pass its JobHandle to ScheduleBatch.
cards/9/q: 100 commands, maxHits = 4. Where do the results of the command at index 7 live, and how far do you read?
cards/9/options/0: From index 28; read up to the first result with collider == null, but no further than 31
cards/9/options/1: From index 7; all commands’ results are laid out back to back
cards/9/options/2: From index 28; read all four, the empty slots are zeroed
cards/9/options/3: From index 700; each command gets 100 slots
cards/9/explain: Command N starts at N × maxHits = 28 and occupies slots 28–31. The first empty slot is marked with collider == null, and the command does not overwrite the ones after it — old contents may remain there.
cards/9/wrong/1: Each command gets maxHits slots, so it starts at N × maxHits.
cards/9/wrong/2: Only the first empty slot is cleared; beyond it there are no guarantees.
cards/9/wrong/3: The array size is commands × maxHits, i.e. 400 slots for all commands.
cards/10/q: You need 2000 “who is inside the blast radius” checks per frame. What do you use?
cards/10/options/0: OverlapSphereCommand.ScheduleBatch: a batch of queries in jobs, results are ColliderHit
cards/10/options/2: 360 RaycastCommands in every direction from each point
cards/10/options/3: An IJobParallelForTransform over every object in the scene
cards/10/explain: Overlaps have their own batches: OverlapSphereCommand, OverlapBoxCommand, OverlapCapsuleCommand (since 2022.2). They work like RaycastCommand: an array of commands, an array of results, ScheduleBatch and a JobHandle.
cards/10/wrong/1: Physics.* is main-thread API; you cannot call it in a job.
cards/10/wrong/2: Rays give an approximation and hundreds of times more queries than needed.
cards/10/wrong/3: That job moves and reads transforms; it does not run physics queries.
cards/11/q: Interviewer: “How do you move 10 000 ordinary GameObjects from jobs?” Which answer is stronger?
cards/11/options/0: One manager instead of 10 000 Updates: a TransformAccessArray created once and a Burst IJobParallelForTransform. I pass time and input in fields, Schedule in Update, Complete in LateUpdate, Dispose in OnDestroy. I keep the objects under different roots: transforms with a shared root go on one thread
cards/11/options/1: I grab each object’s transform right inside an IJobParallelFor
cards/11/options/2: With Parallel.For over a Transform array
cards/11/options/3: I move everything to Entities — there is no other way
cards/11/explain: A strong answer covers the tool, the buffer’s lifetime and the main hierarchy trap. If the interviewer asks “why one thread?”, you have already answered it.
cards/11/wrong/1: Transform is a managed main-thread object; an ordinary job cannot touch it.
cards/11/wrong/2: Transform API may be called only from the main thread; Parallel.For does not change that.
cards/11/wrong/3: Entities is an option, but TransformAccessArray solves this with GameObjects too.
